title: An examination of the quality of kidney stone information on YouTube and TikTok
screen_reason: Content analysis of the top 50 kidney-stone videos on each of YouTube and TikTok (100 videos). Although the paper is framed as a quality appraisal, it reports a separate, explicit binary misinformation variable with counts and denominators (Table 1: YouTube 1/50 = 2%, TikTok 17/50 = 34%), judged by expert reviewers against the American Urological Association kidney stone curriculum as the gold standard. That gives two CONTENT prevalence rows. The Likert quality ratings are additionally captured as QUALITY rows (kept, excluded from prevalence).

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language videos on global platforms; searches run from Ireland on new accounts)
estimates.measure_type: % of the top 50 kidney-stone TikTok videos that contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: The first 50 TikTok videos returned for 'kidney stones' plus 'information, prevention, treatment', sorted by the default 'top' setting, English-language only
estimates.definition: A video was flagged when reviewers identified misinformation in it: claims made in product advertisements, promotion of home remedies and recipes as methods of preventing or treating kidney stones (e.g. avocado seed tea), or claims of cure (e.g. limes), judged against the American Urological Association kidney stone curriculum
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition given; operationalised as content contradicting the American Urological Association's kidney stone curriculum, described in the Discussion as "mostly inaccurate dietary advice, supplements, and the use of exaggerated claims in terms of home remedy effectiveness"
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation was found in 34% of TikTok videos.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 3 of 6; Table 1 ('Misinformation n (%): YouTube 1 (2), TikTok 17 (34)'); also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four independent reviewers rated every video: a consultant urologist, a urology trainee, a medical student and a non-clinical research team member. The two expert reviewers used the American Urological Association's kidney stone curriculum as the 'gold standard'; the two non-expert reviewers rated on their own knowledge. Incidences of misinformation were recorded qualitatively. Kendall's W showed statistically significant agreement on the quality domains for both platforms (strong for YouTube, moderate to strong for TikTok), but the paper reports no reliability statistic for the binary misinformation variable itself and does not say whether a video was flagged on one reviewer's judgement or on consensus.
estimates.moderator_quote: Searches for videos were conducted on 20/03/2024 using the term 'kidney stones' along with the related terms 'information, prevention, treatment'. We searched YouTube and TikTok respectively and new accounts were created on each platform to avoid affecting the results through personalised algorithms. The results were sorted by the default setting of 'relevance' on YouTube and 'top' on TikTok. The first 50 videos were selected for each platform to be reviewed giving a total sample of 100 videos.
estimates.notes: 17/50 = 34%, exactly as reported in Table 1. denom_selection=curated because the corpus is the rank-truncated top 50 search results, not a sample of all kidney-stone videos. The misinformation numerator explicitly includes advertising claims for unevidenced products (18% of TikTok videos contained product advertising, none with supporting research), so it is broader than outright false statements; breadth coded 'misleading'.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language videos on global platforms; searches run from Ireland on new accounts)
estimates.measure_type: % of the top 50 kidney-stone YouTube videos that contained misinformation
estimates.denominator: The first 50 YouTube videos returned for 'kidney stones' plus 'information, prevention, treatment', sorted by the default 'relevance' setting, English-language only, excluding YouTube Shorts
estimates.definition: A video was flagged when reviewers identified overt misinformation in it; the single YouTube case concerned recipes for curing kidney stones, judged against the American Urological Association kidney stone curriculum
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition given; operationalised as content contradicting the American Urological Association's kidney stone curriculum, described in the Discussion as "mostly inaccurate dietary advice, supplements, and the use of exaggerated claims in terms of home remedy effectiveness"
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 3 of 6; Table 1 ('Misinformation n (%): YouTube 1 (2), TikTok 17 (34)'); also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four independent reviewers (consultant urologist, urology trainee, medical student, non-clinical researcher); the two experts benchmarked against the American Urological Association kidney stone curriculum. Kendall's W indicated strong agreement across all 50 YouTube videos on the quality domains; no reliability statistic is given for the binary misinformation variable.
estimates.moderator_quote: 90% of YouTube videos were presented/uploaded by healthcare professionals or an accredited hospital/clinic/journal, whilst for the remaining 10% of videos the information was unavailable. On TikTok 58% of presenters/uploaders were healthcare professionals.
estimates.notes: 1/50 = 2%, exactly as reported in Table 1. The large YouTube/TikTok gap tracks uploader type: 90% of the YouTube videos came from healthcare professionals or accredited hospitals/clinics/journals versus 58% healthcare professionals on TikTok, and no YouTube video contained advertising versus 18% of TikTok videos.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language videos on global platforms; searches run from Ireland on new accounts)
estimates.measure_type: % of the top 50 kidney-stone TikTok videos whose mean reviewer quality rating was 1 out of 5 or lower (very poor quality against the AUA curriculum)
estimates.value_raw: 94% of TikTok videos scored 1/5 or less
estimates.denominator: The first 50 TikTok videos returned for 'kidney stones' plus 'information, prevention, treatment'
estimates.definition: Mean across four reviewers of five-point Likert quality ratings ('very poor quality' to 'very good quality') on general information, epidemiology, presentation/symptoms, treatment and prevention, with a 0 rating where a domain was absent from the video
estimates.misinfo_def: Not applicable: this is a quality score against the American Urological Association kidney stone curriculum, not a truth/falsity judgement
estimates.source_quote: score of 3/5 or more whilst 94% of TikTok videos scored 1/5
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Overall quality of videos', p. 3 of 6
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four reviewers (consultant urologist, urology trainee, medical student, non-clinical researcher) rating five domains on a five-point Likert scale, with the AUA kidney stone curriculum as the benchmark for the expert raters. Kendall's W: strong agreement across all 50 YouTube videos, moderate to strong on TikTok; when restricted to videos that actually contained a given dimension, agreement fell and was no longer significant for symptoms and epidemiology on TikTok.
estimates.moderator_quote: Under each category the quality was rated from 1 (very poor) to 5 (very good). Where there was no information included related to each dimension that video was given a '0' rating.
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, kept but excluded from prevalence per the governing rule: a wholly accurate short video could score 1/5 simply for omitting four of the five curriculum domains (absent domains were scored 0), so a low score is not evidence of falsity. The paper itself attributes much of the TikTok/YouTube gap to TikTok's shorter format covering fewer domains.

estimates.value_raw: Just under half (44%) of YouTube videos received a mean score of 3/5 or more
estimates.denominator: The first 50 YouTube videos returned for 'kidney stones' plus 'information, prevention, treatment'

estimates.misinfo_def: Not applicable: this is a quality score against the American Urological Association kidney stone curriculum, not a truth/falsity judgement
estimates.source_quote: Just under half (44%) of YouTube videos received a mean
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Overall quality of videos', p. 3 of 6
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Four reviewers (consultant urologist, urology trainee, medical student, non-clinical researcher) rating five domains on a five-point Likert scale, benchmarked by the experts against the AUA kidney stone curriculum; Kendall's W indicated strong agreement across all 50 YouTube videos.
estimates.moderator_quote: Mean video quality was significantly higher on YouTube than TikTok, (z=-7.378 p < 0.001). Apart from the prevention category, YouTube had significantly higher scores than TikTok (general information (z=-6.50 p < 0.001), epidemiology (z=-4.79 p < 0.001), symptoms/presentation (z=-6.49 p < 0.001), treatment (z=-7.24 p < 0.001).
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, kept but excluded from prevalence. This is the good-quality direction (3/5 or more), the mirror of the TikTok row's poor-quality direction (1/5 or less); the two are NOT complements of each other and must not be combined. Only 4 of the 100 videos achieved high ratings across all quality categories.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 'over half of videos considered poor quality' (Abstract) is a vaguer restatement of the quality results and was not made into a row. (2) Uploader-qualification and genre shares (Table 1: 22%/58% healthcare professional, 98%/84% educational, 18% of TikTok videos advertising) describe the corpus, not misinformation, though the 18% advertising figure overlaps the TikTok misinformation numerator. (3) 'Overall, 91% of videos were educational in terms of genre' is a genre share across both platforms, not a misinformation share, and it does not match Table 1's per-platform genre counts exactly (49 + 42 = 91 of 100, so 91% is the pooled count). (4) View, like and comment medians and the '46 million views' total are engagement counts without a misinformation denominator, so no exposure-weighted estimate can be built. (5) '58% of KS videos on YouTube had useful information and almost one fifth of videos were misleading' is cited from Sood et al. 2011 (reference 13), a figure the paper takes from elsewhere: excluded by R8. (6) 'up to 88% of individuals seeking health information online and a further 44% making decisions to consult doctors based on online content' is cited from Mohamed and Shoufan (reference 2) and is a health-information-seeking measure, not misinformation exposure: excluded on both grounds. (7) 13 videos were excluded as non-English, so the realised search depth exceeded 50 per platform; the paper does not report from what depth the top 50 were drawn.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Single search on 20 March 2024 for 'kidney stones' plus 'information, prevention, treatment' on YouTube and TikTok, from newly created accounts to limit personalisation; results left in the platforms' default order ('relevance' on YouTube, 'top' on TikTok) and the first 50 English-language videos per platform retained (YouTube Shorts excluded; 13 non-English videos excluded). Four independent reviewers (consultant urologist, urology trainee, medical student, non-clinical researcher) rated each of the 100 videos on five domains using a five-point Likert scale, with absent domains scored 0; the AUA kidney stone curriculum served as the gold standard for the expert raters while the non-experts rated from their own knowledge. Agreement assessed with Kendall's W (strong for YouTube, moderate to strong for TikTok; non-significant for TikTok symptoms and epidemiology once videos lacking that domain were excluded); no reliability statistic reported for the binary misinformation flag and no statement of how reviewer disagreement on it was resolved. Alpha set to p < 0.01 for multiplicity. Rank-truncated, single-country-language, single-time-point sample; the authors note videos beyond the top 100 might be of higher quality.
rob.item6_quote: The expert reviewers (Consultant Urologist and Urology trainee) used the American Urological Association's kidney stone curriculum [14] as the 'gold standard' of information quality. The non-expert reviewers (medical student and non-clinical team member) were instructed to rate the videos based on their own knowledge of the topics in the videos.
